analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal state-run health plan covering every resident, including long-term care benefits.
analysis.headline: The universal health care bill died in committee with one cosponsor and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a universal health plan run by the states: every U.S. resident would be eligible to enroll in an approved health plan with a guaranteed basic benefits package, low-income families would pay nothing out of pocket, and other families' costs would be capped. It also would have set up a national long-term care program covering home care and the first six months of nursing home care, plus new funding for research on AIDS, breast cancer, and other diseases. It was referred to two House committees in March 1990 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident citizen or lawful resident alien would be eligible to enroll in a qualified health plan covering a broad basic package — hospital and physician care, mental health services, drug and alcohol treatment, hospice, prescription-related services, preventive care including mammograms and pap smears, and long-term care [S2][S3]. Families under 200% of the poverty line would pay no premiums or cost-sharing at all, and every family's annual out-of-pocket costs would be capped [S2][S3]. People needing long-term care would get home and community-based services, up to six months of nursing home care, and an optional federal insurance program for longer stays [S2]. Medicare beneficiaries would gain coverage of services Medicare does not pay for [S2]. Older Americans, the disabled, and children would benefit from new research, training, and preventive health grants, plus added funding for AIDS, hypertension, sickle cell anemia, infant mortality, and breast cancer research [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Makes every U.S. citizen and lawful resident eligible to enroll in a state-approved health plan, with a default enrollment process for anyone who shows up for care without coverage.

Guarantees a broad basic benefits package — hospital and physician care, mental health and substance abuse treatment, hospice, preventive screenings including annual mammograms — and forbids plans from limiting the amount or scope of most covered services.

Eliminates premiums and cost-sharing entirely for families under 200% of the poverty line and caps total annual out-of-pocket costs for everyone else at $1,000 for an individual or $2,500 for a family, with community-rated premiums that cannot vary by health status.

Creates a national long-term care program paying for home and community-based care, up to six months of nursing home care, and an optional federal insurance policy for longer nursing home stays, with premium help for low-income people.
Requires providers who take program funds to accept the set payment as payment in full, ending balance billing against patients for covered services.
Authorizes additional research funding for AIDS, hypertension, sickle cell anemia, infant mortality, and breast cancer, and creates geriatric research and training centers.

analysis.who_pays: The bill would be paid for through a mix of federal payments into state Health Security Partnership Funds, required state contributions that could not fall below current levels, and premiums or cost-sharing charged to families above the income limits — up to a $500 deductible and $2,500 per year for larger families [S3]. Providers would bear real cuts in autonomy and income: doctors and hospitals would have to accept the program's set payment as payment in full, hospitals would operate under two-year prospective budgets negotiated with the state, and states would have to develop programs to reduce excess hospital beds and retrain displaced staff [S3]. Private insurers would lose the ability to sell coverage duplicating the basic benefits package [S3].

drawbacks.text: The financing burden falls heavily on the states: each state must fund the program from its own revenues — general funds, taxes, or employer and employee premiums — and may never contribute less than its base-year amount, which could squeeze state budgets or raise state taxes.
Cost-sharing is not abolished: a family could still face a $500 deductible, 20% coinsurance, and up to $2,500 per year in premiums and cost-sharing, a real expense for middle-income households.

Long-term care starts narrow: during an initial phase of two to five years, nursing facility and personal care benefits are limited to people already entitled to Medicare Part A, capped at 90 days per year, and only phase in for the whole population on a timetable the National Board sets.

The benefit package has hard limits that fall on people with serious mental illness: no more than 45 days of inpatient mental health care or 20 outpatient visits per year, and states may further limit substance abuse treatment.

Medicaid would end in any state with an operating program, replacing a defined federal-state entitlement with a state-administered alternative that depends on each state's plan being approved and properly funded.

Implementation is chained to a second hurdle — the program cannot take effect in any year unless at least half the states have passed implementing legislation — a trigger that historically has been difficult to reach.
Banning private insurance that duplicates the basic package would force the restructuring of existing employer-based coverage, a disruptive transition for workers satisfied with their current plans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are enormous on paper: universal eligibility, a generous guaranteed benefit package, no out-of-pocket costs for the poorest families, and the first national long-term care program. The honest cost side is substantial too. The bill leans on state financing with a hard maintenance-of-effort floor, leaves meaningful cost-sharing for middle-income families, starts long-term care with tight limits (Medicare-eligible only, 90 days a year), imposes strict caps on mental health care, and requires half the states to pass implementing laws before anything takes effect. It is a comprehensive but complicated blueprint, and much of the detail — budgets, payment schedules, benefit timetables — would have been worked out by a new federal board and 50 state boards after passage. The bigger question the record answers is not design but support: a bill to remake American health insurance drew exactly one cosponsor and no committee action in ten months.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and their health subcommittees in March 1990, and with only one cosponsor it never got a hearing or a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Rose Oakar introduced the five-division bill on March 1, 1990, naming it for the late Senator Claude Pepper, a decades-long advocate of universal health and long-term care.
Only one member, Rep. Louis Stokes, cosponsored the bill, leaving it with minimal support in a House of 435 members.
The bill was referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees on the day of introduction, and within two weeks both had passed it down to their health subcommittees.
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded for the bill at any point; the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and all work on the bill lapsed with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The congressional committees with jurisdiction over health legislation, which never had to take a position on a bill that would have overhauled health insurance financing, and the existing arrangement of employer-based private insurance, which remained untouched. Americans without health coverage or without long-term care coverage gained nothing from this outcome.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape can only be seen in sponsorship: the sponsor and her one cosponsor were Democrats, and the Democratic-controlled committees to which it was referred took no action before the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill bars private insurance from covering any of the basic benefits package, removing those plans' core product line. In this bill the industry's interest ran against the public's, since its business model depended on selling coverage the bill made universally available through the state plans.

Hospitals would face mandatory assigned payments and state-set biennial prospective budgets, with states required to develop programs to cut excess beds and retrain displaced staff. In exchange, they would gain a universal payer covering virtually every resident, including patients who today cost them money in unpaid care.

Physicians would have to accept plan payments as payment in full and accept state fee schedules tied to a national relative value scale, capping their billing freedom. They would gain a guaranteed payer for all patients but lose pricing power.

industries.industry: Home care and nursing home providers
industries.note: The long-term care division channels federal and state payments through certified home health agencies, case management agencies, and adult day care centers, creating a large new customer base. The bill also entrenches these agencies as permanent gatekeepers: individuals could only receive services through a Case Management Agency's registry and care plan.

HMOs are carved out of state limits on the number of qualified plans, and the National Board is directed to sponsor expansion of organized delivery systems including HMOs. Their growth is written into the design of the program itself.

In states with an operating program, Medicaid would no longer apply, with the new state program taking its place. States would have to maintain their existing spending levels while administering the new financing structure.
